1:
That the estate passed to the queen is explained as law before it is read as providence. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that confiscation of goods necessarily followed a sentence of death in the East, as with ourselves a convicted felon’s property is forfeited to the Crown. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) add that the house of Haman undoubtedly means the house with all that pertained to it. John Gill (reformed) quotes the Targum, which spells out the inventory as the men of his house and all his treasures and all his riches. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) marks the double justice of it, that the goods were justly forfeited to the king and no less justly bestowed by him on the queen, to compensate the danger to which Haman had exposed her.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) turns the transfer into a meditation on property. Thus is the wealth of the sinner laid up for the just, and what Haman would have done mischief with Esther will do good with, since estates are to be valued as they are used. The stewardship that follows shows the vanity of laying up treasure upon earth, for he that heapeth up riches knows not who shall gather them — not only whether he shall be a wise man or a fool, but whether he shall be a friend or an enemy. With what little pleasure, Henry adds, and indeed with what constant vexation, would Haman have looked upon his estate could he have foreseen that the man he hated above all men in the world should have rule over all that wherein he had laboured; it is our interest, therefore, to make sure of those riches which will not be left behind.

How long the kinship had been hidden is noticed as a mark of character. Henry finds Mordecai so humble and modest a man, and so far from being ambitious of a place at court, that though Esther had been four years queen he had concealed his relation to her and her obligations to him as her guardian, and never made use of her interest for any advantage of his own; who but Mordecai, he asks, could have taken so little notice of so great an honour? Wesley says the same of the queen’s side of it, that she had now told how nearly he was related to her, which till this time she had wisely concealed, and that he was admitted into the king’s presence and family and, as it seems, made one of the seven princes.

The ring is weighed as an instrument of state. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) explains that the king’s seal was in the ring, so that giving it to Mordecai was tantamount to giving him the seal of the kingdom, constituting him what a lord chancellor is among us. Ellicott makes him Vizier by the same act, one who would thereby authenticate a royal decree and, having for the time what amounts to a free hand, would save his master all further trouble; and he observes that Mordecai’s position had now become what Daniel’s had been to Darius, that nobler servant to a worthier lord, since he was the queen’s cousin and had once been the means of saving the king’s life, and so starts under distinctly favourable auspices. Keil and Delitzsch supply the constitutional point, that the king’s seal gave the force of law to royal edicts, the seal taking the place of the signature. Gill adds what the ring meant socially, that with the Persians it was a token of the strongest affection and strictest friendship, and that the Targum calls it his signatory ring, with which he signed laws, edicts, letters and patents, so that Mordecai was hereby made keeper of the seals.
3:
Why a second petition was needed is set out first. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) observes that Esther’s work was only half done: she had seen her race’s foe condemned and her kinsman exalted, but the royal edict still stood, and being sealed with the king’s seal was supposed beyond the possibility of alteration; it was not a case in which Mordecai’s new dignity would authorise him to interfere, so Esther, the ice once broken and her courage grown, appeals afresh to the king to do what theoretically lay beyond his power. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) put the legal difficulty plainly: the chief enemy was destroyed, but the edict, having been issued in due legal form, could not according to the laws of the Persians and Medes be revoked.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) weighs the manner of the asking. She came a second time uncalled into the king’s presence, encouraged again by the golden sceptre held out to her, and fell at his feet and besought him with tears, every tear as precious as any of the pearls with which she was adorned, for it was time to be earnest when the church of God lay at stake. Let none be so great as to be unwilling to stoop, he adds, nor so merry as to be unwilling to weep, when thereby they may serve God’s people; and he notices which petition drew the tears, since we read of none when she begged for her own life, but now that she was sure of that she wept for her people, and tears of pity are the most Christ-like.

The wording of the request is admired for its tact. Ellicott finds considerable skill in it, since she avoids speaking of the king’s letters and calls them the device of Haman, which he wrote, while the injury done is laid at the king’s own door, in the destruction of Jews in all the king’s provinces. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the same prudence, that she takes the hatefulness of the action off the king and lays it upon Haman, who had for his own ends contrived the whole business and circumvented the king in it. John Gill (reformed) accounts for the piled-up conditions, that this heap of phrases, all signifying much the same thing, is used to work upon the king’s affections and to show how submissive she was to his will.

The constitutional obstacle divides praise from blame. Henry turns it into an indictment: that no law could be repealed once it had passed the royal assent is so far from bespeaking the wisdom and honour of the Medes and Persians that it bespeaks their pride and folly, since it is ridiculous for any man to pretend to such infallibility as to foresee all the consequences of what he decrees, and unjust to claim such power as to make his decrees irrevocable whether those consequences prove good or bad. This savours, he says, of that old presumption which ruined us all, that we will be as gods; much more prudent is the proviso of our own constitution, that no law can be made unrepealable, since it is God’s prerogative not to repent, and to say what can never be altered. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) states the workaround instead: whatever had passed the royal signet could never be revoked, and no succeeding edict could repeal a preceding one, but one of a similar nature might be enacted, and so the Jews be enabled legitimately to defend themselves, placed on an equal footing with their enemies. Ellicott reads the king’s motive more coolly, that Esther’s device is seen through and he shrinks from so decisive a step as revoking a decree once issued, so does what he can instead: give any orders you please about them, short of repealing the former order.
9:
The two-month delay between the decrees is noticed and accounted for. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) dates Sivan from the new moon in May, so that rather more than two months had passed since the first edict went out, and glosses the officers addressed as satraps. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the interval as discipline: all that time God suffered the Jews to lie under the error of this dreadful day, that they might be the more thoroughly humbled for the sins under which they lay, that they might be convinced of their folly in the many offers they had had of returning to their own country, by which dispersal they had become an easy prey while their brethren in Judea could better preserve themselves, and that his goodness might be the more illustrated in so unexpected a deliverance.

Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) fastens on the languages the decree was published in. It was to be drawn up and sent out in the respective tongues of all the provinces, and from that he turns a question on his own readers: shall the subjects of an earthly prince have his decrees in a language they understand, and shall God’s oracles and laws be locked up from his servants in an unknown tongue? John Gill (reformed) notes only that it was written in the king’s name and sealed with the king’s ring, which gave the letters authority and made them irreversible in their turn.

The beasts that carried it defeat the commentators. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) admits that what these beasts were is difficult to say: the word rendered mules signifies a swift chariot horse, the second is probably Persian but perhaps incurably corrupted, and the third means the sons of mares and is supposed to signify mules bred between the he-ass and the mare. There is so much confusion here, he concludes, and so little consent among learned men, and the true knowledge of them is of so little importance, that we may rest contented with the names our translations give; they were, no doubt, the swiftest and hardiest beasts to be had. Ellicott renders the posts literally as the runners and the mules as horses of great speed, and offers two readings of the disputed pair: with Gesenius, mules the offspring of royal mares, or with Rawlinson, riders upon coursers of the king’s stud, offspring of high-bred steeds.

How far the grant went is the question that matters. Ellicott insists that so far as the edict authorises anything, the Jews are not permitted to take the initiative but merely to stand on the defensive; as it was, it risked civil war in all the cities of the empire, though the results were lessened by the numbers who took the hint the second edict so obviously presented. Of the licence to plunder he notes that when the storm actually came the Jews declined to take advantage of that part of the edict. Clarke argues the parity instead: the terms are the same words as in Haman’s decree, so the Jews had as much authority to slay their enemies as their enemies had to slay them, and since women and children stood in the former grant they must stand in this one. Wesley allows the custom but doubts the practice, holding the clause added to strike the greater terror into their enemies, and observing that we read nothing in the execution of any slaughter of women or children, nor is it probable that men so indulgent as not to meddle with the spoil would have killed innocent children. Henry draws the political moral: the expedient laid the king under a necessity of enacting a civil war in his own dominions, so that both sides took up arms by his authority and yet against it.
15:
The robes are described, then discounted. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) guesses at the blue and white as stripe interchanged with stripe, takes the great crown of gold for a large turban ornamented with gold and jewels, and identifies the fine linen with the byssus of the ancients, supposed to be the tuft growing from the side of a very large muscle found on the Mediterranean coasts, of which a pair of gloves is kept in the British Museum. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) is more exact, noting that the word for crown here is not the one used of a royal crown, and that the garment is the inner tunic, the king’s own being purple striped with white. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) sets no store by any of it except as evidence: these things are not worth notice but as marks of the king’s favour and the fruit of God’s favour to his church, and it is well with a land when the ensigns of dignity are the ornaments of serious piety.

Why the city rejoiced is read generously and cynically. Henry takes Shushan to have been sensible of its own advantage in the preferment, not only pleased with the advancement of virtue but promising itself better times now that so good a man was entrusted with power, since when the wicked perish there is shouting and when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) credits them further, that not only the Jews but the greatest number of the citizens rejoiced, men who by the law of nature abhorred bloody counsels and took complacency in acts of mercy. Ellicott will have none of it: the tide of royal favour had changed, and the people of Shushan were evidently not very different from any populace, who shout with the winning side; nothing succeeds like success, and the crowd of Susa cheered Mordecai as it would doubtless have hooted had it seen him led to execution.

The light the Jews had is read as a figure. John Gill (reformed) reads it as prosperity opposed to the darkness of their adversity, or else as lightsomeness and cheerfulness of spirit. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) agree that light stands figuratively for prosperity, and locate the honour in the joy the inhabitants of Susa showed at the prevention of the threatened destruction. Henry adds what the distress contributed: had they not been threatened they would have had no occasion for such extraordinary joy, so that God’s people are sometimes made to sow in tears that they may reap the more joy, and the suddenness of the turn added much to it, so that they were like those that dream.

The conversions at the end divide the voices sharply. Clarke judges them worthless: these were a species of converts not likely to bring much honour to true religion, though the sacred historian states the simple fact, and they professed Judaism for fear of the Jews, whether they continued steady in that faith or not. From this he turns to his own argument, that it is only the Gospel which will not admit of coercion for the propagation of its doctrines, being a spiritual system propagated only by spiritual influence. Keil and Delitzsch refuse to settle it so fast, holding that the turning of many heathen to Judaism must not be explained only, with Clericus and Grotius, as a change of religion undertaken to procure security and the queen’s favour. Henry allows both motives and adds a third: they thought the Jews great, and counted those happy who were among them, and they thought them formidable, and counted those miserable who were against them; but the holy cheerfulness of those who profess religion is itself a great ornament to it, and it was when the Jews had joy and gladness that many became Jews.
